A land hermit crab (Coenabita clypeatus) sitting at 40-50 % relative humidity is losing water it cannot replace, and most of them die in the shell before the keeper notices. The species does not carry a swimming pool; it carries a water reservoir in its shell, and inside that shell it will tolerate a narrow band of conditions. Most published husbandry targets land somewhere between 70 and 80 % relative humidity, though the often-quoted "80/80" (80 °F and 80 %) is a hobby shorthand rather than a lab finding. What is not contested is that your hydrometer and the sea water in the dish are the two items doing most of the work.

The keeper's diary

Mine was a small crab, maybe 25 mm across the carapace, and on a Thursday evening in February I found it sitting on its back in the corner of the tank with its abdomen half out of the shell. I had a thermometer stuck to the back wall reading 78 °F and a hygrometer reading 72 %, so I thought the air was fine. I checked the water dish and the salt water was gone, but I'd been misting it with the same spray bottle twice a day for three weeks, and the crab had been tipping the dish over. In the end I took two readings: the air at the wall was 72 %, but the air near the substrate was 51 % because the coco fibre had dried out. The crab lived, but its shell lost condition and it did not eat for nine days. The lesson was cheap; the nine days were not.

Setting up the air

The hydrometer you use matters more than the numbers you write down. A cheap dial hygrometer can be 10-15 % out, so buy a digital one and place one probe near the substrate, one in the middle of the tank, and leave both for an hour before you trust anything. Aim for 70-80 % relative humidity, measured near the substrate, and keep the temperature 72-80 °F. If your readings fall short, the usual cause is a ventilated lid or substrate that has dried out. Mist the substrate, not just the air.

Salt water: the part people get wrong

The dish needs to be deep enough for the crab to submerge its shell, but not so deep it can drown. Use a marine mix, not table salt, and make it to 1.023-1.025 specific gravity. A hydrometer is the only way to know this; taste is not a test. Change the salt water every two to three days and keep a second dish of fresh water beside it. When you mix a new batch, measure the specific gravity the same way every time and write the result on the lid. If the crab refuses the salt dish, do not assume it prefers fresh water — it may be too weak to climb in.

The substrate decision

Substrate should be deep enough for a crab to bury itself completely, so start at twice the crab's shell height and build up. A compressed coco fibre block is the most forgiving option and holds moisture well.

Mist correctly by mixing a batch of damp (not soaked) substrate, then checking with the hygrometer after 24 hours. If humidity drops below 60 % overnight, add a second water dish or close part of the lid. If it stays above 85 % for more than a day, you have too little ventilation and mould will follow.

Moulting, and when a refusal to eat is serious

A crab that buries itself and stays down for 2-4 weeks is probably moulting; leave it alone. A crab that stops eating but stays on the surface is a different problem, and usually points to humidity or a shell that is too small. Check the humidity first, then the water dishes, then the substrate dampness. If none of those are wrong, isolate the crab in a small container with damp substrate and watch it for 48 hours. Do not dig up a buried crab to check on it.

Frequently asked questions

My hygrometer reads 55 % overnight — is that dangerous?

A single night at 55 % is unlikely to harm a healthy crab, but repeated drops to that level will. Check the lid, the substrate and the room temperature. A second hygrometer near the substrate usually shows the truth, and the fix is usually a damp substrate block rather than a new tank.

Can I use table salt instead of marine mix?

No. Table salt lacks the calcium and trace minerals a crab needs to balance its shell water, and it will not hold the same specific gravity. Use a marine mix and check it with a hydrometer. Replace the salt water every two to three days, and keep a separate fresh water dish available at all times.

My crab tips its water dish over — what should I do?

Use a heavier, wider dish with a rough ramp and set it into the substrate so the rim is level with the surface. Tipping is usually a climbing behaviour, not spite. If the crab keeps emptying the dish, check whether the salt water is too strong — a crab avoiding a dish is often avoiding a specific gravity problem.
